Prime Number. A natural number greater than one that has no positive divisors other than one and itself.

Primes are the atoms of arithmetic. Every integer factors uniquely into a product of primes. They are central to number theory, cryptography, and the structure of mathematics itself.

The first few primes are two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen, seventeen, nineteen, twenty-three, and twenty-nine. Two is the only even prime. All other primes are odd since even numbers divisible by two cannot be prime. By definition, one is not prime because it lacks a second distinct divisor besides itself. Zero and negative integers are not prime either.

Euclid proved that there are infinitely many primes. This foundational result shows that the primes extend without bound, not merely to some finite limit. The prime number theorem states that the number of primes less than n grows asymptotically as n divided by the natural logarithm of n. This quantifies prime density and shows they become sparser as numbers grow.

The fundamental theorem of arithmetic asserts that every integer at least two factors uniquely, up to order, into a product of primes. This is the bedrock of number theory and the reason primes are called atoms. Mersenne primes have the form two to the p power minus one, where p is prime. Fermat primes have the form two to the two to the n power plus one. Mersenne primes are among the largest known and are actively searched for.

Twin primes are pairs differing by two, like five and seven, or one hundred one and one hundred three. Their infinitude is the open twin-prime conjecture, one of the great unsolved problems in mathematics. The sieve of Eratosthenes is an ancient algorithm for finding all primes up to a given number by iteratively marking multiples of each prime. It remains a practical and elegant method.

A prime's distribution becomes increasingly chaotic. No simple formula generates all primes, though the prime-number theorem provides asymptotic density.
